_🤖_
<!-- Greeting -->
Hey @DataNoob0723! Great to see you diving into the intricacies of LlamaIndex again. How's everything going on your end?

<!-- Answer -->
The `SentenceWindowNodeParser` class in LlamaIndex is designed to split a document into nodes, where each node represents a sentence. Each node also contains a window of surrounding sentences in its metadata. The window size is defined by the `window_size` attribute, which defaults to 3. This means that for each sentence, the parser will include the 3 sentences before and after it in the metadata.

The reason why the first metadata in the `SentenceWindowNodeParser` includes only three items is because it's at the beginning of the document. There are fewer than three sentences before it, so it can only include the sentences that are there. Similarly, the last metadata doesn't include three items because it's at the end of the document. There are fewer than three sentences after it, so it can only include the sentences that are there.

The window size does not include the original text itself. The original text is stored separately in the metadata under the `original_text_metadata_key`. The window only includes the sentences surrounding the original text, not the original text itself. Therefore, the first metadata should include three terms, not four.

This behavior is defined in the `build_window_nodes_from_documents` method:

```py
for i, node in enumerate(nodes):
    window_nodes = nodes[
        max(0, i - self.window_size) : min(i + self.window_size, len(nodes))
    ]

    node.metadata[self.window_metadata_key] = " ".join(
        [n.text for n in window_nodes]
    )
    node.metadata[self.original_text_metadata_key] = node.text
```

In this code, `window_nodes` is a slice of the `nodes` list that includes the sentences surrounding the current node. The `max(0, i - self.window_size)` and `min(i + self.window_size, len(nodes))` expressions ensure that the slice doesn't go beyond the beginning or end of the list. The `window_metadata_key` metadata includes the text of the `window_nodes`, and the `original_text_metadata_key` metadata includes the text of the current node.

You can find more details in the [source code](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-legacy/llama_index/legacy/node_parser/text/sentence_window.py) of the `SentenceWindowNodeParser` class.

Hi @rautaditya2606! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I'm helping the LlamaIndex team.

I can confirm this bug. Looking at the `_clean_text_advanced` method [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/node_parser/text/semantic_double_merging_splitter.py#L388-L398), the issue is exactly as you described — `globals_helper.punkt_tokenizer` is a **sentence** tokenizer (NLTK Punkt), not a word tokenizer. After punctuation is stripped on line 393, the Punkt tokenizer has no sentence-boundary cues left, so it returns the entire text as a single "sentence." The stopword check then compares that whole string against individual stopwords, which never matches.

A fix would be to replace the Punkt sentence tokenizer with simple word-level tokenization, e.g.:

```python
tokens = text.split()
filtered_words = [w for w in tokens if w not in self.language_config.stopwords]
```

Since punctuation has already been removed and the text is lowercased, a plain `str.split()` is sufficient for word tokenization here. There don't appear to be any existing PRs addressing this yet.

I can confirm this bug in the code. The `tool_call_id` fallback at [line 69-70 of utils.py](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/protocols/llama-index-protocols-ag-ui/llama_index/protocols/ag_ui/utils.py#L69-L70) silently fabricates a `uuid4` that has no relationship to any prior `AssistantMessage.tool_calls[*].id`, breaking the pairing invariant that OpenAI/Anthropic providers enforce.

A reasonable fix would be to either:

1. **Raise a `ValueError`** when `tool_call_id` is missing from a `role="tool"` message — making the contract explicit and failing fast rather than silently producing an invalid history.
2. **Attempt to infer** the correct `tool_call_id` from the preceding assistant message's `ag_ui_tool_calls` (if there's exactly one, it's unambiguous), and raise only when inference is impossible.

Worth noting: the reverse function `ag_ui_message_to_llama_index_message` converts tool messages to `role="user"` as a workaround [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/protocols/llama-index-protocols-ag-ui/llama_index/protocols/ag_ui/utils.py#L119-L127), with a TODO acknowledging this is temporary until llama-index-core officially supports tool calls on messages. That conversion faithfully round-trips the fabricated ID back into `additional_kwargs`, which is why the orphan persists across turns as you described.

There's also a related issue in [#22066](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/22066) where `AGUIChatWorkflow.aggregate_tool_calls` only appends `ToolMessage`s for backend tools, orphaning frontend `tool_call_id`s in a similar way [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/22066). These two bugs together suggest the AG-UI tool message pairing logic needs a broader pass.

comments.body:
Hi, I'd like to work on this fix. I've traced through the execution path and confirmed the root cause.

**Root cause (confirmed in source):**

When `AgentWorkflow` runs an agent and it produces no tool calls (i.e., the agent has finished), the workflow's completion handler at `multi_agent_workflow.py` does this:

```python
if not ev.tool_calls:
    agent = self.agents[ev.current_agent_name]  # the FunctionAgent
    output = await agent.finalize(ctx, ev, memory)
    messages = await memory.aget()

    # Only checks the WORKFLOW-level structured_output_fn:
    if self.structured_output_fn is not None:
        output.structured_response = await self.structured_output_fn(messages)
```

The `agent.structured_output_fn` (the per-agent function) is never consulted. The workflow only checks its own `self.structured_output_fn`. Since `FunctionAgent.structured_output_fn` is a proper model field defined in `base_agent.py`, this is a silent mismatch between what the API promises and what actually runs.

By contrast, when `agent.run()` is called directly, the agent's own `structured_output_fn` IS called (in `base_agent.py` line 568), which is why the direct path works but the workflow path does not.

**Proposed fix:**

In the completion handler in `multi_agent_workflow.py`, fall back to the current agent's `structured_output_fn` when the workflow-level one is not set. The `agent` object is already retrieved just above — no extra lookup needed:

```python
if not ev.tool_calls:
    agent = self.agents[ev.current_agent_name]
    output = await agent.finalize(ctx, ev, memory)
    messages = await memory.aget()

    # Use agent-level fn as fallback when workflow-level fn is not set
    effective_fn = self.structured_output_fn or agent.structured_output_fn

    if effective_fn is not None:
        try:
            if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(effective_fn):
                output.structured_response = await effective_fn(messages)
            else:
                output.structured_response = cast(Dict[str, Any], effective_fn(messages))
            ctx.write_event_to_stream(
                AgentStreamStructuredOutput(output=output.structured_response)
            )
        except Exception as e:
            warnings.warn(...)
```

This preserves the existing behavior when `self.structured_output_fn` is set, and adds the missing agent-level fallback.

**Tests I will add:**
- `FunctionAgent` with `structured_output_fn` run via `AgentWorkflow` → callback is invoked
- `AgentWorkflow` with `structured_output_fn` still works as before (regression)
- Both workflow and agent have `structured_output_fn` → workflow-level takes precedence

Could a maintainer please assign this to me? Happy to submit a PR immediately once assigned.

To resolve the 'utf-8' codec decoding error when using `storage_context.persist` with version 0.12.29, you should use the FAISS-specific loading methods instead of the general `StorageContext` approach. Here's how you can do it:

1. Persist the index:
   ```python
   vector_store.persist(persist_path='./storage/faiss_index')
   ```

2. Load the index:
   ```python
   from llama_index.vector_stores.faiss import FaissVectorStore
   import faiss

   faiss_index = faiss.read_index('./storage/faiss_index')
   vector_store = FaissVectorStore(faiss_index=faiss_index)
   ```

This method correctly handles the binary format of FAISS, avoiding the `UnicodeDecodeError` that occurs when using `StorageContext.from_defaults()` <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17887)</sup>.

The 'Permission denied' error you're encountering when using `vector_store.persist` or `FaissVectorStore(faiss_index=faiss_index)` typically occurs due to insufficient file permissions. Here are some potential causes and solutions:

1. **Write Permissions**: Ensure that you have write permissions for the directory where you're trying to save the FAISS index. You can check and modify permissions using your operating system's file manager or command line tools.

2. **Directory Existence**: Verify that the directory specified in your `persist_path` exists. If it doesn't, the `FaissVectorStore` class should create it using `os.makedirs`, but this will fail if you don't have the necessary permissions to create directories in the parent directory.

3. **Read-Only File System**: Ensure that the file system is not mounted as read-only. This can happen with certain external drives or network locations.

4. **File Locks**: Check if the file is being used by another process, which might prevent access.

If these steps don't resolve the issue, you might want to try running your script with elevated permissions (e.g., as an administrator) to see if that resolves the problem.

If `StorageContext` works without issues, it might be worth investigating the specific file handling and permissions required by Faiss in your environment.

Yes, you can create a `VectorStoreIndex` without passing any documents. When you have an existing vector store with data already loaded, you can directly create a `VectorStoreIndex` using the `from_vector_store` method. This method allows you to initialize the index based on the existing data in the vector store, without needing to pass documents initially. Here's an example:

```python
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_vector_store(vector_store=vector_store)
```

This approach leverages the storage capabilities of vector stores, which often persist the entire index (vectors + text) within the store itself, eliminating the need for explicit persistence of the index <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/indices/vector_store/base.py)</sup><sup>[[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/docs/docs/module_guides/storing/customization.md)</sup>.

The issue you're facing with the folder having no content after saving the index with `faiss_vector_store.persist` is likely due to using the incorrect method for persisting the FAISS index. The `faiss_vector_store.persist` method should be used in a way that correctly handles the binary format of FAISS. Here's how you can resolve this:

1. **Persist the Index Correctly**:
   Use the `storage_context.persist()` method to ensure the index is saved properly:
   ```python
   index.storage_context.persist()
   ```

2. **Load the Index Correctly**:
   When loading the index, use the FAISS-specific methods to handle the binary format:
   ```python
   from llama_index.vector_stores.faiss import FaissVectorStore
   from llama_index.core import StorageContext, load_index_from_storage

   vector_store = FaissVectorStore.from_persist_dir("./storage")
   storage_context = StorageContext.from_defaults(
       vector_store=vector_store, persist_dir="./storage"
   )
   index = load_index_from_storage(storage_context=storage_context)
   ```

This approach ensures that the binary format is handled correctly, preventing the need to rebuild the index each time <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17887)</sup><sup>[[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/docs/docs/examples/vector_stores/FaissIndexDemo.ipynb)</sup>.

The `AssertionError` you're encountering during the retrieval process, specifically at the line `assert d == self.d`, indicates a dimension mismatch between the query vector and the vectors stored in the FAISS index. This error typically occurs when the dimensionality of the query vector does not match the dimensionality of the vectors in the index.

Here are some steps to troubleshoot and resolve this issue:

1. **Check Vector Dimensions**: Ensure that the dimensionality of the query vector matches the dimensionality of the vectors stored in the FAISS index. You can print the dimensions of both to verify:
   ```python
   print(f"Query vector dimension: {query_vector.shape[0]}")
   print(f"Index vector dimension: {self._faiss_index.d}")
   ```

2. **Consistent Embedding Model**: Make sure that the same embedding model is used for both indexing and querying. If the model or its configuration changes, it can result in different vector dimensions.

3. **Rebuild the Index**: If there is a mismatch, you may need to rebuild the index using vectors with the correct dimensions. Ensure that all vectors added to the index have the same dimensionality.

4. **Verify Query Vector Construction**: Check how the query vector is constructed and ensure it is done consistently with the vectors in the index. Any preprocessing steps applied during indexing should also be applied during querying.

By ensuring that the dimensions are consistent and that the same embedding model and preprocessing steps are used, you should be able to resolve the `AssertionError` and perform successful queries.

comments.author: Correctover
comments.body:
Encoding errors when loading storage context are **Data Serialization Faults** — and they cause silent data corruption.

After 20,206 API calls, found that encoding issues have three patterns:

1. **Character encoding mismatch**: Data stored with UTF-8, loaded with Latin-1 → characters corrupted → retrieval fails
2. **Binary vs text mode**: Binary data loaded as text → decoding error → file corrupted
3. **Locale-dependent encoding**: System locale changes between save/load → encoding mismatch → data loss

Detection: **Encoding validation** — always specify encoding explicitly (UTF-8). Verify data integrity after load.

Our data: ~10% of "storage context corrupted" complaints are caused by encoding mismatches that weren't detected.

Solution: **Explicit encoding with verification**:
```python
def save_with_encoding(data, filepath, encoding='utf-8'):
    with open(filepath, 'w', encoding=encoding) as f:
        json.dump(data, f)
    
    # Verify save
    with open(filepath, 'r', encoding=encoding) as f:
        loaded = json.load(f)
    if loaded != data:
        raise RuntimeError("Save verification failed")
```

Full taxonomy: https://github.com/Correctover/Correctover/blob/main/docs/fault-taxonomy-v1.md

— Guigui Wang

Good bug report — your diagnosis is correct. Looking at the `StreamingAgentChatResponse` implementation in [`chat_engine/types.py`](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/chat_engine/types.py):

1. **`__str__` only drains the sync `self.queue`** [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/chat_engine/types.py#L138-L144) — it never checks `self.aqueue`, so after async streaming completes the accumulated text is stuck in the async queue.

2. **`awrite_response_to_history` never assigns `self.response`** [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/chat_engine/types.py#L214-L278) — it accumulates `final_text` and writes to memory, but unlike the sync path (which relies on `__str__` draining the sync queue), the final text is never stored back onto `self.response` or `self.unformatted_response`.

A minimal fix would be to add at the end of `awrite_response_to_history` (after line 265, where `self.is_done = True`):

```python
self.unformatted_response = final_text
self.response = final_text.strip()
```

And/or update `__str__` to also drain `self.aqueue` when it's not `None` and not empty:

```python
def __str__(self) -> str:
    if self.is_done and not self.is_function:
        if not self.queue.empty():
            while self.queue.queue:
                delta = self.queue.queue.popleft()
                self.unformatted_response += delta
            self.response = self.unformatted_response.strip()
        elif self.aqueue is not None and not self.aqueue.empty():
            while not self.aqueue.empty():
                delta = self.aqueue.get_nowait()
                self.unformatted_response += delta
            self.response = self.unformatted_response.strip()
    return self.response
```

The simplest and safest approach is probably the first one — assigning `self.response` directly in `awrite_response_to_history` — since that mirrors how the sync `write_response_to_history` relies on consumers draining the queue to populate `response`, but here the async path has no equivalent consumer.

This is a valid bug. Looking at `create_schema_from_function` in [`tools/utils.py`](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/tools/utils.py#L32-L53), the loop iterates over all parameters from `signature(func).parameters` without checking `param.kind`, so `VAR_KEYWORD` (`**kwargs`) and `VAR_POSITIONAL` (`*args`) are treated like regular parameters. Since `**kwargs` has `Parameter.empty` as its default, it gets marked as a required field with type `Any` — which then fails OpenAI's strict mode validation because `Any` has no JSON Schema `type` key.

**Workaround:** You can use `FunctionTool.from_defaults` with the `tool_metadata` parameter to supply a custom `fn_schema` that excludes `kwargs`, or wrap your function without `**kwargs`:

```python
from llama_index.core.tools import FunctionTool

def search(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the web."""
    return _search_impl(query)

tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=search)
```

**Fix:** The proper fix in `create_schema_from_function` would be to skip variadic parameters:

```python
import inspect

for param_name in params:
    if param_name in ignore_fields:
        continue
    if params[param_name].kind in (
        inspect.Parameter.VAR_POSITIONAL,
        inspect.Parameter.VAR_KEYWORD,
    ):
        continue
    # ... rest of the loop
```

This is a straightforward oversight — the function just needs a `param.kind` check to skip `*args`/`**kwargs` before building the schema fields.

comments.author: rajkumar-prog
comments.body:
Hi, I'd like to work on this fix. I've traced through the code and confirmed the root cause.

**Root cause (confirmed in source):**

`create_schema_from_function` in `llama-index-core/llama_index/core/tools/utils.py` builds the Pydantic schema by iterating over `signature(func).parameters`:

```python
params = signature(func).parameters

for param_name in params:
    if param_name in ignore_fields:
        continue
    # ... builds schema field
```

It only skips params listed in `ignore_fields`. It never checks `params[param_name].kind`. Python's `inspect.Parameter.kind` distinguishes five kinds of parameters — `POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD`, `KEYWORD_ONLY`, `POSITIONAL_ONLY`, `VAR_POSITIONAL` (`*args`), and `VAR_KEYWORD` (`**kwargs`).

Because `VAR_KEYWORD` (`**kwargs`) has `Parameter.empty` as its default (no default value), the loop treats it as a required field with type `Any`. Since `Any` has no JSON Schema `type` key, OpenAI's strict mode rejects it immediately with a 400 error.

The same applies to `VAR_POSITIONAL` (`*args`) — it would also be included incorrectly.

**Proposed fix:**

Skip variadic parameters before building the schema field. The `inspect` module is already imported via `from inspect import signature` — we just need to also check `param.kind`:

```python
import inspect

for param_name in params:
    if param_name in ignore_fields:
        continue
    # Skip *args and **kwargs — they have no meaningful JSON Schema representation
    if params[param_name].kind in (
        inspect.Parameter.VAR_POSITIONAL,
        inspect.Parameter.VAR_KEYWORD,
    ):
        continue
    # ... rest of the loop unchanged
```

This is a minimal, targeted change. All normal positional, keyword, and keyword-only parameters are unaffected.

**Tests I will add:**
- Function with `**kwargs` → schema does not include `kwargs` field
- Function with `*args` → schema does not include `args` field
- Function with both `*args` and `**kwargs` → neither appears in schema
- Function with no variadic params → schema unchanged (regression)
- Schema with `**kwargs` no longer fails OpenAI strict mode validation

Could a maintainer please assign this to me? Happy to submit a PR immediately once assigned.

comments.author: m13v
comments.body:
we built a screen capture pipeline for a macOS AI agent and ended up with a similar indexing challenge. a few things from our experience:

for the data connector design, the key decision is granularity. raw OCR frames are too noisy (same text repeated across frames, UI chrome everywhere). what worked for us: deduplicate by content hash per window, only index text that changed between frames, and tag each chunk with app_name + window_title + timestamp. this gives you clean "I was looking at X in Y at time Z" retrieval.

for audio transcription data, segment by speaker turn + silence gaps rather than fixed time windows. a 30-second chunk that spans two different topics is worse than two 15-second topic-coherent chunks.

the time-range filtering is critical for query performance. we store timestamps as the primary index and do a time-bounded search first, then semantic search within that window. "what did I see in Slack yesterday afternoon" should narrow to ~2 hours of data before doing any embedding similarity.

one thing the proposed ScreenpipeReader should handle: deduplication across OCR and accessibility text. if the screen capture OCR'd "hello world" and the accessibility tree also captured "hello world" from the same text field, you don't want both in the index.

**Sync (`_handle_recursive_retrieval`)** uses only `node.hash`:
```python
if not (n.node.hash in seen or seen.add(n.node.hash))
```
[source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/base/base_retriever.py#L177-L182)

```python
if not ((n.node.hash, n.node.ref_doc_id) in seen or seen.add((n.node.hash, n.node.ref_doc_id)))
```
[source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/base/base_retriever.py#L210-L217)

The async version even has a comment explicitly stating `# remove any duplicates based on hash and ref_doc_id`, indicating this was an intentional design decision that wasn't propagated to the sync path.

The fix would be straightforward—update the sync version's deduplication to also use `(n.node.hash, n.node.ref_doc_id)` as the composite key.

- The issue remains unresolved, and you mentioned a PR may address it, with a link to `run-llama/llama_index#20803`.

**Next Steps**
- If this is still relevant on the latest version of the LlamaIndex repository, please let us know by commenting here so the discussion can stay open.
- Otherwise, this issue will be automatically closed in 7 days.

Thanks for your understanding and contribution.

comments.author: joshprzybyszewski-wf
comments.body:
@logan-markewich Thanks for the link!

> Is there a reason to use sync functions with context vars in the first place? 

I have two big assumptions:
1. Using `sync` tools is preferable to using `async`: only use `async` when necessary.
2. `ContextVar`s can be used wherever they make sense to the module's owners to be used.

As the owner of the tool definition, I could choose to always use an `async_fn` input param (even if the backing definition is synchronous), which would avoid this problem, but it would violate my first assumption. Why should I use `async`? Only to avoid a context propagation bug in llama_index internals? How do I codify that new contributors only write `FunctionTool`s that use `async` function definitions (to avoid this same problem)?

For code that I don't own, I don't have the option of avoiding the usage of `ContextVar`s: llama_index internals are dropping the context. For example, OpenTelemetry span context propagation:

https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/blob/dd92fc1934334f0e1f740103bee093ff42cde8ef/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/__init__.py#L38-L51

comments.body: Your suspicion about custom event-loop iteration is almost certainly right — the `fn` branch in `function_tool.py#L78-L80` likely hops through `run_in_executor` or `asyncio.to_thread` without a `contextvars.copy_context().run(...)` wrap, and the OTel context var is exactly the symptom you'd expect. `copy_context().run(self.fn, ...)` inside the sync path should restore parent-span propagation without changing the async branch. <!-- Answer -->
Good catch — this is a confirmed bug. Both `refresh_ref_docs` and `arefresh_ref_docs` in [`BaseIndex`](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/indices/base.py#L429-L482) call `.pop()` on the shared `update_kwargs` dict **inside** the document loop, so the key is removed after the first iteration and all subsequent documents get `{}`.

The fix is to extract the kwargs **before** the loop using `.get()` instead of `.pop()` inside it:

```python
# Before the loop
_insert_kwargs = update_kwargs.get("insert_kwargs", {})
_update_kwargs = update_kwargs.get("update_kwargs", {})

for i, document in enumerate(documents):
    existing_doc_hash = self._docstore.get_document_hash(document.get_doc_id())
    if existing_doc_hash is None:
        self.insert(document, **_insert_kwargs)
        refreshed_documents[i] = True
    elif existing_doc_hash != document.hash:
        self.update_ref_doc(document, **_update_kwargs)
        refreshed_documents[i] = True
```

The same change is needed in the async variant `arefresh_ref_docs`. No existing PR appears to address this yet — a fix would be welcome if you'd like to submit one!

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @jfoerste! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a confirmed bug. The issue is that PR #18447 changed `node_to_metadata_dict()` to use `node.model_dump(mode="json")` instead of `node.dict()` , but `IndexNode` only has a custom `dict()` override [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/schema.py#L886-L903) — it does **not** have a corresponding `@model_serializer` or `model_dump()` override. So when `model_dump()` is called directly, Pydantic's default serialization runs and the `obj` field is serialized without the `__type__`/`__data__` wrapper that `doc_to_json()` would normally add.

On the deserialization side, `IndexNode.from_dict()` still calls `json_to_doc(obj)` [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/schema.py#L928-L935), which expects the `__type__` and `__data__` keys [[3]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/storage/docstore/utils.py#L22-L46). Without them, deserialization fails and falls back to creating a `TextNode` with the raw serialized content as text.

A fix would involve adding a `@model_serializer(mode="wrap")` to `IndexNode` that mirrors the existing `dict()` override logic — wrapping `BaseNode` obj fields via `doc_to_json()`. Something like:

```python
@model_serializer(mode="wrap")
def custom_model_dump(self, handler: SerializerFunctionWrapHandler, info: SerializationInfo) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    from llama_index.core.storage.docstore.utils import doc_to_json

    data = handler(self)
    try:
        if self.obj is None:
            data["obj"] = None
        elif isinstance(self.obj, BaseNode):
            data["obj"] = doc_to_json(self.obj)
        elif isinstance(self.obj, BaseModel):
            data["obj"] = self.obj.model_dump()
        else:
            data["obj"] = json.dumps(self.obj)
    except Exception:
        raise ValueError("IndexNode obj is not serializable: " + str(self.obj))
    return data
```

There are also no existing tests for `IndexNode` round-trip serialization with `BaseNode` obj fields [[4]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/tests/storage/docstore/test_simple_docstore.py), which is why this went undetected.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a confirmed bug. The root cause is in how `AgentWorkflow` initializes state in the context:

**Multi-agent path** (`AgentWorkflow`): stores `initial_state` by direct reference with no copy at all [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/multi_agent_workflow.py#L254):

```python
await ctx.store.set("state", self.initial_state)
```

**Single-agent path** (`BaseWorkflowAgent`): uses a shallow `.copy()` [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/base_agent.py#L228):

```python
await ctx.store.set("state", self.initial_state.copy())
```

So the multi-agent path leaks *all* mutations (top-level and nested), while the single-agent path only leaks nested mutable values (lists, dicts inside the state dict). Neither path uses `copy.deepcopy()`.

A related PR (#20998) previously addressed mutable default arguments causing state leaks [[3]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20998), but the `initial_state` reference issue was not covered.

**Workaround** — until this is fixed, you can avoid leaking by passing a fresh `initial_state` via a factory or by deep-copying it yourself:

```python
import copy

workflow = AgentWorkflow.from_tools_or_functions(
    [bump_counter],
    llm=MockFunctionCallingLLM(),
    system_prompt="...",
    initial_state=copy.deepcopy({"counter": 0}),  # won't help on its own
)

# Option 1: create a new workflow per run
# Option 2: manually reset before each run
workflow.initial_state = {"counter": 0}
```

The fix would ideally be to replace the direct reference with `copy.deepcopy(self.initial_state)` in both paths to fully isolate runs.

Hi @ATOM00blue! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
Good catch. I can confirm this bug exists in `_process_filter_match` in `llama_index/core/vector_stores/utils.py` [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/vector_stores/simple.py#L61-L62). The early `return False` when `metadata_value is None` is applied uniformly to all operators, which is correct for positive operators (`EQ`, `IN`, `GT`, etc.) but semantically wrong for `NE` and `NIN`.

A minimal fix would be to check the operator *before* short-circuiting on `None`:

```python
if metadata_value is None:
    # Missing key trivially satisfies negation operators
    if operator in (FilterOperator.NE, FilterOperator.NIN):
        return True
    return False
```

This aligns `NE`/`NIN` behavior with the logically equivalent `NOT(EQ)`/`NOT(IN)` and matches how several external vector store backends (e.g., Qdrant, LanceDB) already handle missing keys for negative operators [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20374) [[3]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20246).

No existing tests appear to cover this specific case (negation operators + missing metadata key), so adding a test like the repro script above would be valuable.

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @jimhotchkin-wf! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
Thanks for the detailed bug report. I investigated the current state of the code and have some observations:

**The core issue is real, but the details differ from the report.** The current `base.py` has 773 lines total [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse/llama_index/llms/bedrock_converse/base.py), not the ~978+ implied by the report. Also, `ToolCallBlock` does not exist in the LlamaIndex codebase — tool calls are stored as raw dicts in `ChatMessage.additional_kwargs["tool_calls"]`, and the class used downstream is `ToolSelection`.

**What actually happens in streaming:** The streaming code paths (`stream_chat` and `astream_chat`) accumulate the `"input"` field as a concatenated JSON string [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse/llama_index/llms/bedrock_converse/base.py#L434-L440) [[3]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse/llama_index/llms/bedrock_converse/base.py#L594-L600) and yield `ChatResponse` objects with those raw dicts (containing string `"input"`) in `additional_kwargs["tool_calls"]`.

**The `get_tool_calls_from_response` method already handles this correctly** — it checks `isinstance(tool_call["input"], str)` and parses it via `parse_partial_json()` before constructing `ToolSelection` objects with a proper dict `tool_kwargs` [[4]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse/llama_index/llms/bedrock_converse/base.py#L733-L744).

**So the Bedrock Converse adapter itself works end-to-end** because the agent workflow calls `get_tool_calls_from_response()` which normalizes the string. However, the broader concern is valid: if another provider's adapter consumes the raw `additional_kwargs["tool_calls"]` dicts from a Bedrock streaming session (e.g., when persisting and replaying chat history cross-provider), it would encounter string `"input"` values instead of dicts.

**Suggested fix location:** Parsing `current_tool_call["input"]` from string to dict at the `contentBlockStop` event (when the tool use block is complete) would be the cleanest approach. This normalizes the data at the source so all downstream consumers — whether Bedrock's own `get_tool_calls_from_response` or another provider — see a dict. This is a one-line addition per streaming method rather than touching 6 construction sites.

comments.author: ayushh0110
comments.body:
Opened #21580 to fix this.

Instead of parsing at `contentBlockStop` as suggested by Dosu, I went with a `_parse_tool_input()` helper applied at each of the 6 `ToolCallBlock` construction sites. The `contentBlockStop` approach has a couple of issues — there's no handler for that event in the current code, and even if we added one, intermediate `contentBlockDelta` yields would still emit raw strings before it fires. The helper approach normalizes every yield (intermediate and final), requires no new event handlers, and matches the existing defensive pattern already used in `get_tool_calls_from_response()`.

comments.author: rehan243
comments.body:
The fix is pretty straightforward - we just need to parse that `tool_call["input"]` string to a dict before passing it to `ToolCallBlock`. We can use `json.loads()` for this. Here's what the corrected code might look like:
```python
import json
# ...
ToolCallBlock(
    tool_kwargs=json.loads(tool_call.get("input", "{}")),
    tool_name=tool_call.get("name", ""),
    tool_call_id=tool_call.get("toolUseId"),
)
```
We've run into similar issues with other providers where the API returns JSON strings that need parsing - took us a few tries to catch all the edge cases. Are you using the latest boto3 version (1.34.x or newer)?

comments.author: ayushh0110
comments.body: Thanks @rehan243 ! I've already addressed this in #21580 — same core idea but wrapped in a defensive helper with fallback for partial JSON during intermediate streaming yields, applied across all 6 construction sites.

comments.author: hanselhansel
comments.body: Confirming this exact failure mode shows up the moment chat history gets replayed across providers. We hit the string-vs-dict mismatch when a multi-agent workflow had Bedrock streaming on the planner side and Google GenAI on the executor side, and the executor failed schema validation on the replayed tool call. The defensive helper approach in #21580 is the right shape because the alternative (parse at the consumer) means every downstream provider has to know about Bedrock's streaming quirk forever. Normalizing at the adapter boundary is what keeps this from becoming a contract negotiation between every pair of providers. One small ask for the helper: does it also handle the partial-JSON case where an intermediate `contentBlockDelta` yield emits a half-string? The PR description suggests yes, which is the right call, but a unit test pinning that behavior would save the next person tracing a flaky test back to half-parsed JSON.

Different code path from the half-value case in most JSON parsers, and the one I have seen leak through helper-level tests because the value-side fixture covers the obvious failure.

For the `_ContextManagerWrapper` ImportError with weaviate-client v4.20.5:

This is a compatibility issue between llama_index and newer weaviate versions. The `_ContextManagerWrapper` class was removed or renamed in weaviate-client v4.20.x.

try:

    from weaviate.collections.classes.internal import _ContextManagerWrapper

Or update the dependency constraint: `weaviate-client>=4.5,<4.20`

Thanks for the detailed report. Looking at the current LlamaIndex `google_genai` integration, the file handling in `utils.py` unconditionally uses `types.Part.from_bytes()` for all `DocumentBlock` content regardless of file size or whether VertexAI is configured [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-google-genai/llama_index/llms/google_genai/utils.py#L204-L212). The VertexAI config is resolved in `base.py` and passed to the `google.genai.Client` constructor [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-google-genai/llama_index/llms/google_genai/base.py#L166-L178), but this configuration isn't consulted when processing file content — so users hit the cryptic downstream error from the `python-genai` SDK with no context about why it failed.

A fix here could add a check in the `DocumentBlock` handling path: if VertexAI is enabled and the file exceeds 20MB (the threshold where `from_bytes` triggers a file upload under the hood), raise a clear error explaining that file uploads aren't supported with VertexAI and suggesting inline mode or reducing file size. The relevant code to modify is in [`llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-google-genai/llama_index/llms/google_genai/utils.py`](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-google-genai/llama_index/llms/google_genai/utils.py#L204-L212) around the `DocumentBlock` handling.

@strawgate  Sorry, it seems that I made a mistake while testing it, probably used a venv with the old dependency in it. Testing it again today I'm still getting the same error with 0.12.52 as the default raise_error is True for the **get_node** function in **BaseDocumentStore** even if we pass False to the **get_nodes** (note the plural here), so the configuration is not respected.

```
def get_node(self, node_id: str, raise_error: bool = True) -> Optional[BaseNode]:
        """
        Get node from docstore.

        Args:
            node_id (str): node id
            raise_error (bool): raise error if node_id not found

        """
        doc = self.get_document(node_id, raise_error=raise_error)

        if doc is None:
            # The doc store should have raised an error if the node_id is not found, but it didn't
            # so we raise an error here
            if raise_error:
                raise ValueError(f"Node {node_id} not found")
            return None

        # The document should always be a BaseNode, but we check to be safe
        if not isinstance(doc, BaseNode):
            raise ValueError(f"Document {node_id} is not a Node.")

        return doc
```

Code from **get_nodes** that doesn't use the raise_error value when calling **get_node** if it's False:
```
if raise_error:
            return [node for node_id in node_ids if (node := self.get_node(node_id, raise_error=True))]
        else:
            return [self.get_node(node_id) for node_id in node_ids]
```

I tried modifying the code passing the raise_error value to False there:
```
if raise_error:
            return [node for node_id in node_ids if (node := self.get_node(node_id, raise_error=True))]
        else:
            return [self.get_node(node_id, raise_error=False) for node_id in node_ids]
```

And then we get the expected None value from that function but then it fails in the **_insert_fetched_nodes_into_query_result** function in **VectorIndexRetriever** class when it tries to build the id to nodes dict
```
        fetched_nodes_by_id: Dict[str, BaseNode] = {
            str(node.node_id): node for node in fetched_nodes
        }
```
As node is None this fails with an AttributeError accessing the node_id property.

Modifying that line to check for None values fixes that issue and we get the response and the source node back:
```
        fetched_nodes_by_id: Dict[str, BaseNode] = {
            str(node.node_id): node for node in fetched_nodes if node is not None
        }
```

<!-- Answer -->
I couldn't find a specific issue related to the `PydanticUserError` you're encountering, but there is a related issue regarding Pydantic v2 changes. In Pydantic v2, the `__modify_schema__` method is not supported, and you should use the `__get_pydantic_json_schema__` method instead. This method is used to generate a JSON schema for a Pydantic model and includes customizations for the schema <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/types.py)</sup><sup>[[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/schema.py)</sup>.

For the `SecretStr` class, ensure that any schema modifications are done using the `__get_pydantic_json_schema__` method. This change is part of the transition from Pydantic v1 to v2, which may have affected your code.

Additionally, there were several changes made in the `llama_index` package to support Pydantic v2, such as fixing validation errors and handling nested models <sup>[[3]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/docs/docs/CHANGELOG.md)</sup>. You might want to check if these changes are relevant to your issue.

If the problem persists, consider reviewing the implementation of the `SecretStr` class and related schema methods to ensure compatibility with Pydantic v2.

Hey, @myvaheed! 👋 I'm here to help you with any bugs, questions, or contributions you have for llama-index. Let's squash those bugs together!

<!-- Answer -->
The issue you're encountering with the stepwise execution in the Llama Index workflow seems to be related to synchronization problems between `WorkflowHandler.run_step()` and `Workflow._start()._task()`. The use of `await asyncio.sleep(0)` in the `run_step` method can indeed yield control back to the event loop prematurely, leading to potential deadlocks when the `_step_condition` is notified before the workflow is ready to handle it.

This synchronization issue can cause the `run_step` method to never complete, as you've described in your test case. The problem arises because the notification of `_step_condition` happens before the workflow is prepared to process the next step, leading to a deadlock situation.

Regarding the future support for stepwise execution, the current implementation has known limitations, such as not supporting human-in-the-loop scenarios with stepwise execution <sup>[[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/workflow/workflow.py)</sup>. It would be beneficial to check for updates or fixes in future releases of the Llama Index library that might address these synchronization issues.

Additionally, you've pointed out a documentation error regarding the stepwise execution, which should be corrected to reflect the actual behavior and usage of the handler in the workflow.

For now, you might consider implementing a workaround by ensuring that the workflow's steps are properly synchronized or by avoiding the use of `await asyncio.sleep(0)` in contexts where it could lead to premature yielding.

comments.author: dosubot[bot]
comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
This is a real and already-tracked gap that affects multiple providers, not just Anthropic. Here's what's going on:

**The issue is actually two-layered:**

1. **Anthropic LLM layer**: The Anthropic integration stores thinking content in `additional_kwargs["thinking"]` as accumulated `ThinkingBlock` objects, rather than populating `additional_kwargs["thinking_delta"]` with incremental deltas like Ollama, OpenAI, and BedrockConverse do [[1]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-anthropic/llama_index/llms/anthropic/base.py). So even if the agent layer looked for `thinking_delta`, it wouldn't find it from Anthropic.

2. **Agent workflow layer**: `AgentStream` currently has **no `thinking_delta` field at all** [[2]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/workflow_events.py#L23-L30), and the agent workflows (`FunctionAgent`, `ReActAgent`, `CodeActAgent`) don't extract thinking content from `ChatResponse.additional_kwargs` when creating `AgentStream` events [[3]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/function_agent.py#L64-L72). So even providers that *do* set `thinking_delta` (Ollama, OpenAI, BedrockConverse) have their thinking content silently dropped at the agent level.

**Related issues already tracking this:**

- [#20063](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20063) — Inconsistent thinking streaming across all providers [[4]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20063#issuecomment-3953809596)
- [#20349](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20349) — BedrockConverse `thinking_delta` not visible in `AgentStream` [[5]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20349)
- [#21232](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/21232) — Ollama drops thinking-only chunks during streaming [[6]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/21232)

Maintainers have acknowledged this and mentioned plans to add streaming content blocks as a unified API to replace the current `additional_kwargs` approach [[7]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20063#issuecomment-3953809596#L50-L55), but there's no implementation yet.

**Workaround for now**: You can access thinking content from the `raw` field on `AgentStream` events, which contains the underlying `ChatResponse`. For Anthropic specifically, look in `event.raw.additional_kwargs["thinking"]` or the raw Anthropic response objects with `ThinkingDelta` blocks. It's not as clean as a first-class field, but it's the only path currently available at the agent layer.

<!-- Answer -->
Thanks for reporting this! I can confirm this is a real bug in the [delete_nodes() method](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/indices/document_summary/base.py#L259-L262). The issue is a classic Python antipattern—mutating a list while iterating over it:

```python
for node in node_ids:
    if node not in index_nodes:
        logger.warning(f"node_id {node} not found, will not be deleted.")
        node_ids.remove(node)  # BUG: Mutating list during iteration
```

When `remove()` is called, the iterator doesn't adjust, causing it to skip the next element. That's why `does_not_exist_1` gets filtered but `does_not_exist_2` slips through and causes the KeyError.

A simple fix would be to iterate over a copy or use list comprehension:

```python
valid_node_ids = []
for node in node_ids:
    if node not in index_nodes:
        logger.warning(f"node_id {node} not found, will not be deleted.")
    else:
        valid_node_ids.append(node)
node_ids = valid_node_ids
```

I didn't find an existing PR addressing this specific bug, so this issue should help get it tracked. Similar KeyError fixes have been applied to other index types ([#19476](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/19476), [#19448](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/19448)), but not yet to `DocumentSummaryIndex`.

text=chat_response.message.content or "",

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @ynyyn! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a valid bug. The root cause is in [`get_format_string()`](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/output_parsers/pydantic.py#L53) which calls `json.dumps(schema_dict)` without setting `ensure_ascii=False`. By default, `json.dumps()` uses `ensure_ascii=True`, which escapes all non-ASCII characters.

The fix would be changing line 53 from:
```python
schema_str = json.dumps(schema_dict)
```
to:
```python
schema_str = json.dumps(schema_dict, ensure_ascii=False)
```

This is consistent with how other parts of LlamaIndex have handled similar issues—for example, [PR #20266](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20266) made the same change to `node_to_metadata_dict` to preserve readable Unicode in vector stores.

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @Yermy311! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a confirmed bug, and you're not the first to encounter it. The issue is related to how the formatter template is selected during initialization.

**Root Cause:** When `ReActChatFormatter.from_defaults()` is called without a `context` value, it selects `REACT_CHAT_SYSTEM_HEADER` (which has no `{context}` placeholder). Even though there's a [post-validation mechanism](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/react_agent.py#L48-L62) that tries to sync `system_prompt` to `formatter.context`, it can't inject context into a template that doesn't have the placeholder for it.

**Better Workaround:** Instead of subclassing, you can pass the formatter explicitly with the correct template:

```python
from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import ReActAgent
from llama_index.core.agent.react.formatter import ReActChatFormatter
from llama_index.core.agent.react.prompts import CONTEXT_REACT_CHAT_SYSTEM_HEADER

agent = ReActAgent(
    tools=tool_list,
    llm=llm,
    system_prompt="your system prompt here",
    formatter=ReActChatFormatter.from_defaults(system_header=CONTEXT_REACT_CHAT_SYSTEM_HEADER)
)
```

This ensures the formatter uses the template that includes the `{context}` placeholder, allowing the post-validator to properly inject your `system_prompt`.

Related issues: [#19156](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19156), [#20416](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20416)

<!-- Answer -->
Thanks for the detailed bug report! I can confirm this is a real issue in the codebase.

Looking at the [stream_chat implementation](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/chat_engine/condense_plus_context.py#L342-L375), the memory writes are placed *inside* the wrapped generator after the streaming loop completes:

```python
def wrapped_gen(response: StreamingResponse) -> ChatResponseGen:
    full_response = ""
    for token in response.response_gen:
        full_response += token
        yield ChatResponse(...)
    
    # Memory writes happen here - AFTER streaming completes
    self._memory.put(ChatMessage(content=message, role=MessageRole.USER))
    self._memory.put(ChatMessage(content=full_response, role=MessageRole.ASSISTANT))
```

So if the stream isn't fully consumed, the generator never reaches those `put()` calls. [ContextChatEngine uses the same pattern](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/chat_engine/context.py#L240-L385).

Note: I couldn't find `MultiModalCondensePlusContextChatEngine` or `MultiModalContextChatEngine` in the codebase—those may not exist or might be named differently.

Related: there's also [issue #17801](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17801) tracking a separate bug where `astream_chat()` can drop memory writes even when streams *are* fully consumed due to asyncio task references not being held.

comments.author: weiguangli-io
comments.body:
## Root Cause Analysis

I've traced through the source code to confirm the root cause and want to add some deeper technical context and concrete fix proposals.

### The Core Problem: Side Effects Inside a Generator

In `CondensePlusContextChatEngine.stream_chat()`, the `wrapped_gen` inner function is a Python **generator** — its body executes lazily, only advancing when the caller calls `next()`. The `memory.put()` calls are placed *after* the `for token in response.response_gen` loop:

```python
def wrapped_gen(response: StreamingResponse) -> ChatResponseGen:
    full_response = ""
    for token in response.response_gen:
        full_response += token
        yield ChatResponse(...)

    # These lines execute ONLY if the for-loop above exhausts naturally
    self._memory.put(user_message)
    self._memory.put(assistant_message)
```

This is a well-known footgun with Python generators: **any code after the last `yield` is a finalizer that only runs if the generator is fully consumed or explicitly `.close()`'d — and `.close()` raises `GeneratorExit` inside the generator, which skips past the post-loop code entirely.** So there is no execution path that reaches those `memory.put()` calls when the stream is interrupted.

This same pattern exists in:
- `ContextChatEngine.stream_chat()` (context.py L263-L277)
- `MultiModalCondensePlusContextChatEngine.stream_chat()` (multi_modal_condense_plus_context.py)
- `MultiModalContextChatEngine.stream_chat()` (multi_modal_context.py)
- All corresponding `astream_chat()` async variants

### Contrast: Engines That Get This Right

Notably, `CondenseQuestionChatEngine.stream_chat()` and `SimpleChatEngine.stream_chat()` handle this differently:

1. **`SimpleChatEngine`** writes the user message to memory *eagerly before streaming*, then spawns a background `Thread` calling `write_response_to_history()` which consumes the stream and writes the assistant message. This ensures the user message is never lost.

2. **`CondenseQuestionChatEngine`** follows the same thread-based pattern — it calls `self._memory.put(user_message)` immediately, then delegates assistant-message persistence to `StreamingAgentChatResponse.write_response_to_history()` in a thread.

These two engines are resilient to partial consumption because the user message is persisted synchronously and the assistant response is written by a dedicated consumer thread.

---

## Proposed Fix Strategies

### Option 1: Eager User Message + `try/finally` for Assistant Message (Recommended)

Write the user message **before** returning the generator. Use `try/finally` inside the generator to guarantee the assistant message is persisted with whatever content was streamed so far:

```python
def stream_chat(self, message, chat_history=None):
    synthesizer, context_source, context_nodes = self._run_c3(
        message, chat_history, streaming=True
    )
    response = synthesizer.synthesize(message, context_nodes)

    # Persist user message eagerly — this is always safe
    self._memory.put(ChatMessage(content=message, role=MessageRole.USER))

    def wrapped_gen(response):
        full_response = ""
        try:
            for token in response.response_gen:
                full_response += token
                yield ChatResponse(
                    message=ChatMessage(content=full_response, role=MessageRole.ASSISTANT),
                    delta=token,
                )
        finally:
            # Runs on normal completion, break, or .close()
            if full_response:
                self._memory.put(
                    ChatMessage(content=full_response, role=MessageRole.ASSISTANT)
                )

    return StreamingAgentChatResponse(
        chat_stream=wrapped_gen(response),
        sources=[context_source],
        source_nodes=context_nodes,
        is_writing_to_memory=False,
    )
```

**Trade-offs:**
- (+) Minimal change, easy to review
- (+) Consistent with how `SimpleChatEngine` already handles it
- (+) `finally` in generators is well-defined in Python (PEP 342) — `GeneratorExit` triggers it
- (-) A partially-streamed assistant message gets saved. This is arguably *correct* behavior (the LLM did generate those tokens, and the user did see them), but some users may want to distinguish partial from complete responses.

### Option 2: Thread-Based Consumer (Align with SimpleChatEngine)

Refactor to match the `SimpleChatEngine`/`CondenseQuestionChatEngine` pattern exactly: persist the user message eagerly, then use `StreamingAgentChatResponse.write_response_to_history()` in a background thread with `is_writing_to_memory=True`.

**Trade-offs:**
- (+) Full consistency across all chat engines
- (+) Leverages existing, tested infrastructure (`write_response_to_history` already handles edge cases)
- (-) Introduces threading, which adds complexity and may interact poorly with non-thread-safe memory backends
- (-) Requires rethinking how `wrapped_gen` and `write_response_to_history` interact to avoid double-consumption of the generator

### Option 3: Provisional Memory with Completion Marker

Introduce a concept of "provisional" memory entries that are written eagerly but marked as incomplete. A flag or wrapper could indicate whether the turn completed:

```python
self._memory.put(user_message, provisional=True)
# ... after stream completes ...
self._memory.confirm(user_message)
```

**Trade-offs:**
- (+) Most semantically correct — downstream consumers can distinguish complete from partial turns
- (-) Requires changes to the `BaseMemory` interface, which is a much larger API surface change
- (-) Over-engineered for most use cases

---

## Recommendation

**Option 1** is the pragmatic choice — it's a minimal, localized fix that solves the data-loss problem without introducing new abstractions or threading. The `finally` block in a generator is the Pythonic way to handle cleanup, and it's exactly what the language provides for this class of problem.

For the async variants (`astream_chat`), the same pattern applies — `try/finally` inside an async generator works identically (PEP 525).

I'd also suggest adding a `is_partial: bool` metadata field to `ChatMessage` in a follow-up, so memory consumers can optionally distinguish partial from complete responses without needing full provisional-memory semantics.

Happy to submit a PR if the maintainers agree on the approach.

<!-- Answer -->
Your analysis is correct. The root cause is in [PR #20664](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20664)'s `extract_thinking_from_block()` function in `utils.py`, which only extracts the `text` field from `reasoningContent` and completely ignores the `signature` field:

```python
if "reasoningContent" in block:
    reasoning = block["reasoningContent"]
    if "reasoningText" in reasoning:
        return reasoning["reasoningText"].get("text")
    return reasoning.get("text")  # Only extracts text, ignores signature
```

When a streaming chunk contains only a signature (like `{"reasoningContent": {"signature": "...."}}`), this function returns `None`, causing the signature to be dropped. AWS Bedrock then rejects the incomplete thinking block with the ValidationException you're seeing.

This is a known issue area — [Issue #20349](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20349#issuecomment-3633482669) documents that `reasoningContent` blocks can contain a `signature` field that must be preserved for Bedrock's validation.

**Workaround**: As a temporary workaround, you can extract thinking content directly from raw event data: `event.raw['contentBlockDelta']['delta']['reasoningContent']['text']`.

**Required Fix**: The `extract_thinking_from_block()` function needs to be updated to handle both `text` and `signature` fields from `reasoningContent` to properly support extended thinking with tools.

The issue is in [`IngestionPipeline.run()` at lines 505-517](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/ingestion/pipeline.py#L505-L517) where it directly mutates `self.docstore_strategy` instead of using a local variable:

self.docstore_strategy = DocstoreStrategy.DUPLICATES_ONLY  # This permanently changes the instance

The fix centralizes docstore operations in `_update_docstore()` and `_aupdate_docstore()` methods that handle strategy logic without mutating the instance variable.

If you're on v0.14.15, you may need to upgrade to a version that includes these fixes. As a **workaround** for older versions, you can re-set the strategy before each run:

```python
pipeline.docstore_strategy = DocstoreStrategy.UPSERTS
pipeline.run(documents=[...])

Looking at the code, `chat_engine` should be automatically initialized via a Pydantic field validator called [`chat_engine_from_query_pipeline`](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-cli/llama_index/cli/rag/base.py#L153-L176) when `RagCLI` is instantiated. If `chat_engine` remains `None`, it likely means one of these validators failed silently during instantiation. Possible causes:
1. **Invalid or missing `ingestion_pipeline`** — the validator chain depends on a valid ingestion pipeline
2. **Exception in validators being swallowed** — if validators raise an exception, `chat_engine` would stay `None`
3. **Pydantic version incompatibility** — different versions handle field validators differently

Could you share the full stack trace? That would help pinpoint where the initialization is failing. Also, confirming your Pydantic version would be helpful since validator behavior can vary between versions.

comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
You're right—`FaissMapVectorStore.from_persist_path` currently uses `eval()` to deserialize the persisted id map, which is unsafe since it can execute arbitrary code if the file is tampered with. The proposed fix in [PR #20675](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20675) replaces this with `json.dump`/`json.loads` for safe serialization, and adds an `ast.literal_eval` fallback to maintain backward compatibility with files saved using the old `str()` format. The PR also normalizes key types after loading, since JSON converts all dict keys to strings but FAISS expects integer keys. This PR is open and not yet merged, so the unsafe `eval()` usage remains in the main branch for now. Until the fix lands, it's best to avoid modifying persisted id map files and consider patching your local code to use `ast.literal_eval` or `json` for deserialization if you need a safer workaround.

This is a known issue caused by a legacy typo: TextNode defines metadata_seperator (with an "e"), which overrides the correctly spelled metadata_separator from BaseNode. BaseNode uses a Pydantic alias so both spellings are accepted during initialization, but in TextNode only metadata_seperator is actually used for content generation. This leads to inconsistent behavior—Document supports both variants interchangeably, but TextNode only respects the "e" variant, even though both attributes are present on the instance. The typo is preserved in TextNode for backward compatibility with serialized objects and is not intentional design, just a legacy artifact. No recent changes address this, so for version 0.14.13, always use metadata_seperator when working with TextNode to ensure your separator is applied as expected. More context: [see here](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/schema.py#L315-L1196), [and here](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17258).

Hi @MarioRicoIbanez! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
You're correct—SchemaLLMPathExtractor currently generates Pydantic schemas with `additionalProperties: true` for optional Dict fields, which leads to incompatibility with both GPT-5-mini (which requires `false`) and Gemini (which rejects the field entirely). This is a known issue and is not yet fixed in the core implementation; the schema is built dynamically and there is no built-in logic to clean or patch the generated JSON schema for compatibility with these APIs [(source)](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/indices/property_graph/transformations/schema_llm.py#L132-L339).

Your workaround—subclassing SchemaLLMPathExtractor and patching `model_json_schema` to clean `additionalProperties`—is the recommended approach for now. This pattern is also used elsewhere in LlamaIndex, for example in the Gemini integration, where a helper recursively removes all `additionalProperties` fields before sending schemas to the API [(reference)](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20123). This does not drop critical type information, only a validation constraint that Gemini and some OpenAI models do not support.

Other schema generation components in LlamaIndex that use Dict fields or `extra='allow'` in Pydantic models are affected by the same issue. The best practice for structured output APIs is to avoid Dict fields in your schemas when possible, or always clean the schema before sending it to the LLM API.

If you need a reusable utility, you can adapt the cleaning logic from the Gemini integration or your own workaround. Until an official fix lands in LlamaIndex core, patching the schema as you described is the way to go.

**Proposed Fix:**
```python
if entity_dicts:
    for entity_dict in entity_dicts:
        self.structured_query(
            f"""
            MERGE (e:`__Entity__` {{id: $data.id}})
            SET e += $data.properties
            SET e.name = $data.name
            WITH e, $data.properties.triplet_source_id AS tsid, $data.embedding AS embedding
            SET e:{entity_dict["label"]}
            WITH e, tsid, embedding
            CALL {{
                WITH e, embedding
                WITH e, embedding
                WHERE embedding IS NOT NULL
                SET e.embedding = vecf32(embedding)
                RETURN count(*) AS count
            }}
            WITH e, tsid
            WHERE tsid IS NOT NULL
            MERGE (c:Chunk {{id: tsid}})
            MERGE (e)<-[:MENTIONS]-(c)
            """,
            param_map={"data": entity_dict},
        )
```

<!-- Answer -->
Your proposed Cypher fix is correct for FalkorDB: extracting `triplet_source_id` as `tsid` before the `CALL {}` block ensures the variable is available for the subsequent `MERGE` statements, which resolves the silent failure in relationship creation. This approach matches Cypher scoping rules and is a known workaround for FalkorDB's limitations with nested parameter access after subqueries.

One thing to note: the current FalkorDB test suite only verifies MENTIONS relationships when created explicitly via `upsert_relations`, not automatically via `upsert_nodes` when an entity has a `triplet_source_id`. To fully validate your fix, you should add a test that upserts a chunk and entities (with `triplet_source_id`), then asserts that the MENTIONS relationships are created as expected—similar to the pattern used in the Nebula property graph store tests [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20401).

No side effects or regressions are expected from this change, as it only alters variable scoping in the query and does not affect other logic. This fix will make FalkorDB's behavior consistent with other supported graph stores.

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @binaryblood! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
This isn't a bug—BM25Retriever needs access to the raw text nodes, but vector stores like ChromaVectorStore only store embeddings, not the original text. That's why you get a ValueError: the BM25 implementation receives an empty corpus when you pass a VectorStoreIndex backed by Chroma, so it can't build its keyword index ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19527), [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19910)).

The semantic retriever works because it uses the vector store for retrieval, which is compatible with ChromaVectorStore. BM25Retriever, on the other hand, expects a list of nodes (documents with text).

You have two main options:

**1. Pass nodes directly to BM25Retriever**

Keep your list of Document objects (or nodes) and use them directly:

```python
from llama_index.retrievers.bm25 import BM25Retriever

# After you create your documents list
retriever = BM25Retriever.from_defaults(
    nodes=documents,  # pass your list of Document objects here
    similarity_top_k=5
)
```

**2. Store nodes in the docstore with store_nodes_override=True**

When creating your index, set `store_nodes_override=True` so the docstore is populated and BM25Retriever can access the text:

```python
index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(
    documents,
    storage_context=storage_context,
    embed_model=embed_model,
    store_nodes_override=True
)
retriever = BM25Retriever.from_defaults(index=index, similarity_top_k=5)
```
Note: If you use this option, you are responsible for persisting the docstore if you want to reload it later ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19527)).

**Limitations:**  
- BM25Retriever does not support non-ASCII tokenization or UTF-8 encoding well in older versions, and has limitations with languages like Chinese and Japanese ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17461#issuecomment-3485167473)).
- For hybrid retrieval (semantic + keyword), you need to ensure both the vector store and the raw text nodes are available.

Let me know if you want a full code example for your specific setup!

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @Roaimkhan! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
You're right—llm_retry_decorator doesn't support async methods properly. It always returns a synchronous wrapper, so when you decorate an async method, it loses its coroutine status (e.g., asyncio.iscoroutinefunction returns False), which breaks async behavior and retry logic for those methods. This is a known issue and has been confirmed in recent discussions and merged PRs, but the decorator hasn't been updated to handle async functions yet ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17967), [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20544)).

A recommended workaround is to use an explicit async retry helper inside your async methods instead of a decorator. For example:

```python
import asyncio

async def async_retry(func, *args, retries=3, backoff=1, **kwargs):
    attempt = 0
    while True:
        try:
            return await func(*args, **kwargs)
        except Exception:
            if attempt >= retries:
                raise
            await asyncio.sleep(backoff * (2 ** attempt))
            attempt += 1
```

Then, call this helper from your async method:

```python
async def _achat(self, ...):
    return await async_retry(self._real_achat, ...)
```

For a decorator that supports both sync and async functions, the best practice is to check if the wrapped function is a coroutine using inspect.iscoroutinefunction and return an async wrapper if so, otherwise a sync wrapper ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20517)). Here’s a minimal example:

```python
import functools
import inspect

def retry_decorator(f):
    @functools.wraps(f)
    async def async_wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        # async retry logic here
        return await f(*args, **kwargs)

    @functools.wraps(f)
    def sync_wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        # sync retry logic here
        return f(*args, **kwargs)

    return async_wrapper if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(f) else sync_wrapper
```

There’s no official fix yet, so keep an eye on related issues and PRs for updates. For now, use the helper pattern above for async retries.

You're right—the current implementation of `to_openai_message_dict` always sets `"detail": "auto"` in image blocks, even when `block.detail` is `None`. This isn't required by the OpenAI API and causes compatibility issues with OVH endpoints, which reject the `"detail"` field entirely if present. The recommended fix is to update the code so that `"detail"` is only included when `block.detail` is not `None`. This change would align with the OpenAI spec and resolve the 422 errors you encountered with OVH-hosted models. There are no recent merged PRs or inline comments addressing this, and the current behavior appears to be intentional but not strictly correct for all OpenAI-like endpoints. You can see the relevant code and context [here](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-openai/llama_index/llms/openai/utils.py#L319-L435).

Making this change should not affect other integrations, as the OpenAI API itself allows the omission of `"detail"` when not needed.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a known issue: when the LLM returns an empty message, the ReActAgent's take_step method raises a ValueError and crashes the workflow. This happens intermittently and is not tied to a specific model or configuration—it's triggered any time the model streams zero data or produces an empty response. There is currently no built-in retry or graceful fallback for this in the framework, and recent updates have not addressed it yet ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19924), [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19288), [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/workflow/react_agent.py#L111-L153)).

If you need to avoid workflow crashes, you have a few options:

- Implement custom retry logic by subclassing or wrapping the agent, so you can catch the empty message error and retry or handle it gracefully ([example discussion](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19392)).
- Consider switching to FunctionAgent, which is less prone to this specific crash in some setups ([workaround suggestion](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17629)).
- Double-check your LLM configuration (like max_tokens and streaming settings), as sometimes upstream model issues or misconfigurations can cause empty outputs ([maintainer comment](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17629)).

There is no official fix or built-in workaround as of the latest releases. If you need help sketching out a custom handler or want to discuss a workaround for your specific workflow, let me know!

This is a confirmed bug in llama-index-postprocessor-nvidia-rerank==0.5.1: the code only checks if the instance is "hosted" to decide whether to include the Authorization header, so on-prem setups that require an API key do not send it, causing authentication failures. However, since `_api_key` defaults to `'NO_API_KEY_PROVIDED'`, the most robust patch is:

```python
_headers = self._get_headers(
    auth_required=bool(self._api_key and self._api_key != "NO_API_KEY_PROVIDED") or self._is_hosted
)
```

This ensures the header is only sent when a real API key is present or when hosted, avoiding dummy headers for unauthenticated setups. There are no other places in the module that need this change, and no existing issues or merged PRs address this bug yet. You can safely patch your local installation with this logic to resolve the problem.

This crash happens because the custom Thread class always sets the thread target to copy_context().run, which requires a callable as its first argument. When target=None, no callable is passed, so you get a TypeError instead of the standard library's "do nothing" behavior. This is inconsistent with Python's threading.Thread, where target=None is valid and safe to use. You can see this in the implementation: if target is None, args is set to an empty tuple, so copy_context().run is called with no arguments, causing the crash ["llama_index/core/types.py#L148-L176"](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/types.py#L148-L176).

As a workaround, you can avoid using llama_index_core.types.Thread with target=None, or subclass it and override __init__ to skip setting the target to copy_context().run when target is None. This would make its behavior match the standard library and prevent the crash. No official fix or workaround exists in the current codebase.
