<!-- Answer -->
This is a confirmed bug in the truncate_text implementation: when max_length is less than 3, the function slices with a negative index and appends '...', resulting in output longer than max_length. There’s no special handling for small max_length values, so the function violates its intended contract in this case. This is not intentional and is due to missing logic for small values [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/utils.py#L348-L353).

There’s no official fix or workaround in the codebase or discussions. As a workaround, you can wrap the function like this:

```python
def safe_truncate_text(text, max_length):
    if max_length <= 3:
        return text[:max_length]
    from llama_index.core.schema import truncate_text
    return truncate_text(text, max_length)
```

This will ensure the output never exceeds max_length for very small values.

This error happens because the ChatMessage model in LlamaIndex enforces that if a message contains multiple blocks (like a TextBlock and a ToolCallBlock), you can't use the .content property directly—you have to work with the .blocks property instead. The conversion logic in ag-ui is trying to set message.content, which triggers the ValueError when there are multiple blocks present [see explanation](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20184).

A fix for this was merged after your version (v0.14.12): the code now sets message.blocks to a list containing a single TextBlock, instead of trying to set message.content [see PR #19954](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/19954). To resolve this, you can either upgrade to a version that includes this fix, or manually update your code to manipulate the blocks property when handling multi-block ChatMessages.

If you need to convert messages with multiple blocks from other formats, LlamaIndex provides utilities like from_openai_message_dict to help build ChatMessage objects with the blocks field populated, preserving the block structure [see usage example](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20382).

Hi @Atlas4285! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
You're right—there's currently no fallback or timeout for NLTK data downloads in offline or sandboxed environments. The code tries to use the NLTK_DATA environment variable, or defaults to a static cache directory within the package, but if the required data isn't found, it attempts to download it and will block if the network is unavailable. There's no logic to check multiple cache locations, copy the static cache, or set a download timeout, so this can cause long hangs in restricted environments. The maintainers have acknowledged this issue and discussed fixes, but as of now, the most reliable workaround is to set the NLTK_DATA environment variable to a directory containing the required NLTK data before running your application. This ensures the package uses your pre-populated cache and avoids triggering downloads or blocking behavior. See more details and maintainer comments [here](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19661) and [here](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19913).

The current implementation of mean_agg does not handle empty input explicitly—it passes the empty list to numpy's mean, which returns nan (a float), not a list. This violates the function's type hint (List[float]) and can cause downstream TypeErrors if code expects a list. There are no comments or documentation specifying intended behavior for empty input, and no existing issues or PRs address this case. Best practice would be to either raise a clear exception or return an empty list when input is empty, to maintain type consistency and avoid hard-to-debug errors. You can see the implementation here: [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/base/embeddings/base.py#L27-L49).

comments.body: Hi, I'd like to submit a fix for this. The root cause is in _separate_thinking() - when the Mistral API returns structured ContentChunk objects (ThinkChunk + TextChunk), the method only extracts ThinkChunk text and then tries to match <think> regex tags on it. Since structured chunks don't contain raw tags, the regex never matches, so thinking text gets returned as the response and the actual TextChunk response is lost. The fix splits the logic: regex-based parsing for raw string responses (streaming path), and direct chunk type separation for structured List[ContentChunk] responses (non-streaming path). Will open a PR shortly.

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @AkshitGulyan! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a known pitfall with ReActAgent in 0.12.30: if your updated system prompt is missing required template variables (like `{tool_desc}` and `{tool_names}`), or if you format the prompt string too early, the agent can silently fail and stop making LLM calls—no errors, just nothing happens. This is because the formatter expects those variables to be present and will leave unreplaced placeholders if they're missing, which breaks downstream logic without raising exceptions ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/agent/react/formatter.py#L51-L104)).

**How to fix:**
- Make sure your custom system prompt includes all the variables used in the default, especially `{tool_desc}` and `{tool_names}`.
- When updating, pass the *template* string (with placeholders), not a pre-formatted string. For example:
  ```python
  react_system_prompt = PromptTemplate(
      "You are an assistant.\nAvailable tools: {tool_names}\n{tool_desc}\n[Your extra instructions here]"
  )
  agent.update_prompts({"react_header": react_system_prompt})
  agent.reset()  # Ensures the new prompt is used
  ```
- Do **not** call `.format()` on your prompt string before wrapping it in `PromptTemplate`—let the agent/formatter handle the formatting at runtime.

**Tip:** You can validate your prompt before updating to avoid silent failures:
```python
def validate_prompt_vars(custom_prompt, default_prompt):
    if set(custom_prompt.template_vars) != set(default_prompt.template_vars):
        raise ValueError(f"Custom prompt must have variables: {default_prompt.template_vars}")

default_prompt = agent.get_prompts()["react_header"]
validate_prompt_vars(react_system_prompt, default_prompt)
```
([reference](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/18479))

**Other gotchas:**  
- Avoid markdown code block quotes (```) in your prompt—they can break model behavior ([reference](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17796)).
- Always call `agent.reset()` after updating prompts to refresh the agent's state ([reference](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/18163)).

If you follow these steps and ensure your prompt template matches the default's variables, your agent should resume making LLM calls as expected.

Hi @d2726725460-cmyk! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a confirmed bug: passing an int as the second argument to `faiss.IndexIDMap.add_with_ids` is incorrect and causes the `AttributeError` you saw. The Faiss API expects a 1-D numpy array of int64 ids (shape `(n,)`, dtype `np.int64`) matching the number of vectors being added. The correct usage is to pass, for example, `np.array([self._faiss_index.ntotal], dtype=np.int64)` as the second argument when adding a single vector. The `delete` method in the same class already uses this pattern for `remove_ids`.

To fix the bug, update the call to:

```python
self._faiss_index.add_with_ids(
    text_embedding_np,
    np.array([self._faiss_index.ntotal], dtype=np.int64)
)
```

This ensures the ids argument matches the expected type and shape for Faiss operations, and will resolve the error you encountered.  
[Reference](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/vector_stores/llama-index-vector-stores-faiss/llama_index/vector_stores/faiss/map_store.py#L112-L140)

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @amaheshar! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
The error happens because ChromaVectorStore expects every retrieved node to have valid text content, even for image-only nodes. When an image node with no text is returned, it tries to create a TextNode with `text=None`, which triggers the Pydantic ValidationError since TextNode requires a string for the text field. This is a limitation in how ChromaVectorStore reconstructs nodes from metadata and content—it doesn't distinguish image nodes from text nodes during retrieval, so image-only nodes cause failures [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/vector_stores/llama-index-vector-stores-chroma/llama_index/vector_stores/chroma/base.py#L406-L484).

MultiModalVectorStoreIndex is designed to keep text and image nodes separate, but ChromaVectorStore's retrieval logic doesn't fully support this distinction yet. True multi-modal support (where text and images are interleaved or jointly embedded) is not fully implemented in LlamaIndex and would require significant refactoring [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19753).

**Workarounds:**  
- Store text and image embeddings in separate ChromaDB collections and only query the appropriate collection for each modality.
- Filter out image-only nodes from text queries, or ensure that every node in the text collection has a valid string in its text field.
- For multi-modal retrieval, combine results from separate queries to text and image collections in your application logic.

Recent updates have focused on multi-modal chat/query engines, but have not yet fixed this specific validation error for image-only nodes in ChromaVectorStore [source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20265). If you need robust multi-modal support, keep an eye on future releases and ongoing work in this area.

Let me know if you want code examples or more details on structuring your collections or retrieval logic.

```bash
pip install langchain==0.3.0
```

There’s currently no migration guide or patch for LangChain 1.x support in llama-index-llms-langchain. If you need LangChain 1.x features, consider using other LlamaIndex integrations (like llama-index-llms-ollama) or writing a custom adapter. response_txt += delta["content"]

```python
response_txt += delta.get("content") or ""
```

Do the same when yielding the `delta` field in `ChatResponse`:

```python
yield ChatResponse(
    message=ChatMessage(
        content=response_txt,
        role=response_role,
        additional_kwargs={"tool_calls": tool_calls},
    ),
    delta=delta.get("content") or "",
    raw=line,
)
```

<!-- Answer -->
This happens because generic Pydantic models like `GenericDataModel[int]` generate a schema title with brackets (e.g., `GenericDataModel[int]`), but OpenAI's API requires the schema name to match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`—so brackets and similar characters aren't allowed. LlamaIndex passes the schema title directly to OpenAI without sanitizing it, which causes the 400 error you see when using generics with `as_structured_llm` [see code reference](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-openai/llama_index/llms/openai/utils.py#L743-L755).

To work around this, set a valid schema title on your generic model using Pydantic's config, for example:

```python
class GenericDataModelInt(BaseModel):
    answer: int

    class Config:
        title = "GenericDataModelInt"
```

Or, for Pydantic v2:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class GenericDataModelInt(BaseModel):
    answer: int
    model_config = ConfigDict(title="GenericDataModelInt")
```

This will ensure the schema name is valid for OpenAI and avoid the error.

Hi @RiccardoRubini! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
This is a limitation of how OpenAIResponses in LlamaIndex interacts with the OpenAI Responses API. When `store=False` (the default), reasoning steps (like "thinking") are not persisted server-side, so if a subsequent tool call references that reasoning step by ID, you get a 400 error about the item not being found. When you set `store=True`, the API expects the reasoning item to have a required follow-up (like encrypted content or a summary); if that's missing, you get a different 400 error about missing follow-up items. The LlamaIndex wrapper just forwards the `store` flag and doesn't handle these edge cases or rehydrate missing items, so chaining reasoning and tool calls without storing everything isn't currently supported in this integration. There are no built-in workarounds or recent fixes for this in LlamaIndex as of now. For more details, see the [OpenAIResponses implementation](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-openai/llama_index/llms/openai/responses.py#L214-L866).

I'd like to work on this.

After analyzing the codebase, I found the root cause is in `to_openai_responses_message_dict()` function in `utils.py`. When reasoning items are serialized for the API input, they're sent as ID references only, which causes issues because:

1. With `store=False`: OpenAI doesn't persist reasoning items, so ID references fail
2. With `store=True`: Reasoning items need to be properly paired with their following items

**Proposed fix**: Instead of sending reasoning items as ID references, we should either:
- Omit reasoning items from the conversation history input entirely (since they represent internal model thinking)
- Or properly structure the reasoning items with their required following items according to OpenAI's API spec

comments.author: dosubot[bot]
comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
This happens because only gemini-2.5-pro supports structured prediction via the Google GenAI API in a way that LlamaIndex expects: it returns a parsed BaseModel when you provide a response_schema. The flash and flash-lite models (including 2.0 and 2.5 variants) do not populate response.parsed, even if response.text contains valid JSON. The LlamaIndex integration checks for response.parsed and raises a ValueError if it's missing, which is why you see this error for those models. There is no model-specific workaround in the codebase—this is a limitation of the Gemini API and model capabilities, not a bug in LlamaIndex itself ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/llms/llama-index-llms-google-genai/llama_index/llms/google_genai/base.py#L513-L637)).

If you need structured output from flash/flash-lite models, you can manually parse response.text as JSON when response.parsed is None, or use prompt engineering to encourage valid JSON output. Some users adapt the streaming structured prediction logic (which tries to repair and parse partial JSON) for non-streaming use cases, but this is not built into the main structured_predict method. Community discussions confirm that this is a known limitation and not considered a bug in LlamaIndex ([discussion](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/18392)).

The 30-second timeout is enforced by the MCP-Client itself. Even if you set higher timeout values in your agents or workflows, the BasicMCPClient defaults to a 30-second session timeout unless you explicitly set the timeout parameter when creating the client. This value is passed to the underlying session as `read_timeout_seconds`, and if not set (or if set incorrectly), the client will terminate the task after 30 seconds and send a DELETE to the MCP-Server, regardless of progress notifications—they do not extend or reset the timeout [[source]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/20270).

In your code, you are setting `timeout=600` when creating the BasicMCPClient, which should override the default. If you are still seeing a 30-second timeout, double-check that the value is actually being passed through and not being overridden elsewhere. There are no hardcoded 30-second limits in the agent or workflow layers—they just forward the timeout parameter to the workflow base [[source]](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-integrations/tools/llama-index-tools-mcp/llama_index/tools/mcp/client.py#L97-L248).

If the problem persists, make sure you are not accidentally creating a BasicMCPClient somewhere else in your code without the timeout parameter, and that the correct client instance is being used by your tool spec.

If httpcore logs show 30s, that's the value actually being enforced, regardless of what you set elsewhere. 

So yes, httpcore's timeout is the reason for the 30s cutoff and DELETE, and the user-supplied timeout isn't being propagated as expected in your current setup.

<!-- Answer -->
This issue is caused by how FunctionAgent handles tool calling: even in non-streaming mode, it uses the LLM's async streaming interface (`astream_chat_with_tools`). For gemini-3-pro-preview, this can result in no response or tool calls unless streaming is enabled, because the model's API may not reliably emit events unless a streaming session is active. This is why your lower-level call to `llm.achat_with_tools` works (it uses the non-streaming path), and why enabling streaming on the agent resolves the problem.

Recent changes in [PR #20207](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20207) updated Gemini tool calling logic, but the agent's architecture still relies on streaming internally, even if you don't request streaming. This difference in code paths explains the behavior you're seeing.

As a workaround, you can either use streaming mode with FunctionAgent, or stick to direct calls to `llm.achat_with_tools` for non-streaming scenarios with gemini-3-pro-preview. If you need non-streaming agent orchestration, you may need to adapt the agent to use the non-streaming LLM interface for Gemini models.

comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
You’re right—there’s a corner case in the Memory class’s `_manage_queue` logic where, if the token limit and flush size are set low enough, the active queue can end up with only an assistant message remaining. The code does try to maintain conversation integrity by keeping the first message as a user message, but if only one message fits after flushing, and it’s an assistant reply, there’s no safeguard to restore a preceding user message. This can cause errors with providers like Amazon Bedrock that require the first message to be from the user. You can see the relevant logic and its limitations in the source code [here](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/memory/memory.py#L626-L756).

A related issue discusses that translating flushed messages into a single string (as done in the vector memory block) could help increase compatibility across providers that have strict requirements on message order—see the discussion [here](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19841).

For now, if you need to avoid this, you may want to ensure your token limits and flush sizes are set so that at least one full user→assistant turn remains in the queue, or consider patching the flushing logic to always preserve a user message as the first active message.

<!-- Answer -->
You're correct—this is a design inconsistency. For ChatMode.CONTEXT and ChatMode.CONDENSE_PLUS_CONTEXT, the chat engines built by MultiModalVectorStoreIndex use response synthesizers that are text-only, even when the index is multimodal. This causes images and other non-text data to be ignored or lost in responses. In contrast, ChatMode.SIMPLE and ChatMode.CONDENSE_QUESTION use a query engine that supports multimodal data, which is why they work as expected.

Recent changes in the repository, including the removal of multi-modal LLM integrations, may further impact or limit multimodal capabilities in these chat modes ([PR #20161](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20161)). There isn't a built-in workaround for enabling multimodal support in CONTEXT or CONDENSE_PLUS_CONTEXT modes at this time. If multimodal responses are critical, using ChatMode.SIMPLE or ChatMode.CONDENSE_QUESTION is currently the most reliable approach. 

You may want to monitor future updates for improvements or changes to multimodal support in chat engines.

<!-- Answer -->
You're correct—currently, VectorIndexRetriever generates a query embedding whenever self._vector_store.is_embedding_query is True, without checking vector_store_query_mode. This means embeddings are created even for TEXT_SEARCH mode, leading to unnecessary API calls, especially with stores like OpenSearch. The vector_store_query_mode is stored but not used in the embedding generation condition, so your proposed conditional would prevent this issue and is a sound workaround for now. 

Regarding QueryFusionRetriever, in sync mode (_retrieve), the embedding is set once and reused for all retrievers. In async mode (_aretrieve), each retriever independently generates the embedding, causing redundant calls for the same query due to the lack of shared state between async tasks. This matches your observations and explains the test failures you saw when switching to async behavior.

No recent pull requests address this specific issue, so your workaround is currently the best approach. If you want to avoid unnecessary embedding generation, update the condition as you suggested:

```python
if self._vector_store.is_embedding_query and self._vector_store_query_mode in (VectorStoreQueryMode.DEFAULT, VectorStoreQueryMode.SEMANTIC_HYBRID):
    # calculate query embedding
```

References:  
[VectorIndexRetriever embedding logic](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/indices/vector_store/retrievers/retriever.py#L66-L117)

comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
The error is happening because the ChatMessage object's blocks field must contain valid ContentBlock objects, each with a block_type discriminator (like "text" or "image") for Pydantic to validate them correctly. If you pass a string, a ChatMessage, or a dict that doesn't have block_type, you'll get the union_tag_not_found error.

To fix this, make sure you construct your messages like this:

```python
from llama_index.core.llms import ChatMessage, MessageRole, TextBlock

messages = [
    ChatMessage(
        role=MessageRole.USER,
        blocks=[TextBlock(text="What is the capital of France? answer short.")]
    )
]
resp = llm.stream_complete(messages)
```

You can also use the content argument for backward compatibility, which will automatically wrap your string in a TextBlock:

```python
messages = [
    ChatMessage(role=MessageRole.USER, content="What is the capital of France? answer short.")
]
resp = llm.stream_complete(messages)
```

Both approaches ensure the blocks field is populated with a valid ContentBlock (with block_type="text"), which resolves the validation error. More details on the expected schema and the role of block_type are in the codebase and recent PRs ([source](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/base/llms/types.py)).

comments.body:
<!-- Answer -->
This error is likely due to a mismatch between the expected input format for `stream_complete` and how the message objects are being constructed or passed in your current version. In LlamaIndex, each block in a `ChatMessage` must be an instance of a block class (like `TextBlock`) that has a `block_type` field set, and the list of blocks should not contain nested `ChatMessage` objects or other types without `block_type`—otherwise, Pydantic can't validate them and you'll see the `union_tag_not_found` error ([reference](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/ddeb22219e1255829d07cde44e172c8f8c6bd2ff/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/base/llms/types.py)).

In some cases, especially with certain versions, you may need to serialize your message objects before passing them to the LLM. Try converting your messages to dictionaries using `.model_dump()`:

```python
messages = [
    ChatMessage(
        role=MessageRole.USER,
        blocks=[TextBlock(text="What is the capital of France? answer short.")]
    )
]
resp = llm.stream_complete([msg.model_dump() for msg in messages])
```

If this still doesn't work, there may be a version-specific bug or a breaking change in how message schemas are validated ([see related issue](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/17291)). Recent PRs have addressed similar problems by ensuring blocks are explicitly set as lists of block instances, not appended or nested ([see PR](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20207)). If you're on 0.14.7 and still seeing this, it may be worth checking if upgrading to the latest release resolves the issue.

Let me know if serializing with `.model_dump()` works or if you see a different error!

<!-- Greeting -->
Hi @OmriAckerman! I'm [Dosu](https://go.dosu.dev/dosubot) and I’m helping the llama_index team.

<!-- Answer -->
You are correct: PR #20104 changed the schema creation logic to always execute `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS`, which requires the `CREATE` privilege even if the schema already exists. This breaks least-privilege setups where the user only has USAGE/ALL on an existing schema. The PR was intended to address SQL injection risks but did not account for this privilege escalation and was released as a patch, not a breaking change. There are currently no tickets or documentation acknowledging this issue or discussing a fix.

Your suggested approach—to revert to a check-first pattern (querying `information_schema.schemata` before attempting to create the schema) or using `inspect(engine).get_schema_names()`—matches the logic used in previous versions and is feasible. The check-first pattern avoids requiring the CREATE privilege when the schema already exists, which aligns with least-privilege principles.  
You can see the relevant code and discussion in [PR #20104](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/20104).

comments.author: OmriAckerman
comments.body:
@logan-markewich The schema is created **beforehand** by a database administrator/superuser as part of the deployment setup, following the principle of least privilege:

**Deployment workflow:**
1. DBA/superuser creates the schema (has CREATE privilege)
2. DBA grants USAGE + ALL PRIVILEGES on the schema to the application user
3. Application user does NOT need CREATE privilege on the database - only rights within the existing schema

This is a standard security pattern to limit application privileges. The application only needs:
- USAGE on the schema
- ALL PRIVILEGES on tables/objects within the schema
- NOT CREATE privilege on the database itself

**The issue:** v0.4.2 always attempts `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS`, which requires CREATE privilege even when the schema already exists (and PostgreSQL checks permissions before evaluating IF NOT EXISTS).

**v0.4.1 behavior (working):** Checked if schema exists first, only attempted CREATE if missing
**v0.4.2 behavior (broken):** Always runs CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS, fails with "permission denied"

The fix would be to check `inspect(engine).get_schema_names()` first, and only run CREATE if the schema is missing.

<!-- Answer -->
You're right—up through v0.14.3, FunctionTool.from_defaults only used the first line of a multi-line docstring for the tool description, with no built-in way to override this behavior. This led to incomplete descriptions being sent to the LLM, as you described.

This limitation has since been addressed. As of PR #19532 (merged July 2025), FunctionTool.from_defaults now parses and includes parameter descriptions from the full docstring, supporting Sphinx, Google, and Javadoc docstring styles. The tool description now includes the function signature, the first meaningful line as a summary, and detailed parameter descriptions extracted from the docstring. The function schema is also enriched with these descriptions if not already present. Tests were added to verify this behavior across different docstring formats. You can see the implementation details and examples in the merged PR: [#19532](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/pull/19532).

If you're on an older version, the only workaround is to manually provide the description. Upgrading to a version including or after this PR will give you the improved docstring handling.
